title: AI on Both Sides of the Fight
mindset: AI doesn't invent new crimes; it makes old ones faster, cheaper and more convincing, so defenders must verify, not just recognise.

cards.title: What changed with AI
cards.body: Before AI, a convincing scam email took effort: good grammar, local details, a believable tone. Now a chatbot writes a perfect one in seconds, in any language, tailored to you. AI is a **force multiplier**: like giving every burglar a master locksmith's apprentice. The attacks are mostly the familiar ones (phishing, fraud, recon). What changed is **speed, scale and polish**.

cards.title: Phishing without the typos
cards.body: We used to teach 'look for spelling mistakes'. That advice is now outdated. AI-written phishing is fluent, uses your company's style, and can reference real projects scraped from LinkedIn. The new rule: judge a message by **what it asks you to do** (pay, log in, share, hurry), not how it looks. Urgent requests for money or credentials get verified through a **second, known channel**.

cards.title: Deepfakes: seeing is no longer believing
cards.body: AI can clone a voice from a short clip and fake a face on a video call. Criminals use this for **CEO fraud**: 'It's the boss, I need an urgent transfer.' The defence isn't spotting glitches; fakes keep improving. It's **process**: call-back on a known number, a shared code word for urgent money requests, and two-person approval for payments.

cards.title: How defenders use AI
cards.body: Security teams drown in alerts. AI helps by **summarising** logs, **triaging** alerts (which ones look like real attacks?), explaining malware behaviour, and drafting incident reports. Google, Microsoft and others build AI into security tools. The golden rule: AI is an **assistant, not an authority**. It can be wrong confidently, so analysts verify before acting.

cards.title: The defender's mindset shift
cards.body: When anything can be faked (text, voice, video, a login page), trust must come from **verification**, not appearance. That means MFA that resists phishing (passkeys/security keys), out-of-band confirmation for money and access requests, and logging so you can investigate later. Ask yourself: 'If this message were AI-generated, what would stop me acting on it?'

attacks.name: Deepfake-enabled payment fraud
attacks.analogy: A con artist who can borrow your boss's face and voice for a phone call.
how: Attacker gathers public video/audio of an executive (talks, interviews).
They create a convincing voice or video imitation with AI tools.
They contact finance staff with an urgent, secret request to move money.
Pressure and authority push the employee to skip normal checks.
attacks.thinking: "People trust faces and voices they recognise, and they rarely question the boss under time pressure."
attacks.signs: Unusual urgency or secrecy, new bank details, requests outside normal process, refusal to allow a call-back, odd timing.
attacks.defend: Mandatory call-back on a known number, two-person approval for payments, code words for urgent requests, staff training that 'the boss' can be faked.

story.title: Arup deepfake video call (2024)
story.body: In early 2024, a finance employee at the engineering firm Arup in Hong Kong joined a video call with what appeared to be the company's CFO and several colleagues. All of them were AI-generated deepfakes. Convinced, the employee made a series of transfers totalling about **US$25 million**. Lesson: when faces and voices can be faked, payment safety must come from **process** (independent verification and multi-person approval), not from recognising people.

lab.title: Build your personal 'verify, don't trust' checklist
lab.goal: Practise judging messages by what they ask, and set up phishing-resistant sign-in on your own accounts.
steps: Open your email spam folder and pick 3 suspicious messages (don't click links).
For each, write: what does it want me to DO? What's the pressure trick (urgency, authority, fear, reward)?
Check the real sender address in the full headers.
Turn on a passkey or authenticator-app MFA for your most important account (email first).
Agree a family/team code word for urgent money requests.

commands.explain: Creates a notes folder and opens a simple text editor so you can write your checklist. Save with Ctrl+O, exit with Ctrl+X.
If you save a suspicious email as `suspicious.eml`, this shows the real sender lines. A Reply-To that differs from From is a classic red flag.

lab.safety: Never click links or open attachments in suspicious emails while analysing them. Use only your own mailbox. Creating deepfakes of real people without consent can be illegal; this lab is about defence only.

hunt:
Your finance colleague gets a WhatsApp voice note from 'the CEO': perfectly his voice, asking to pay a supplier's new bank account today 'before the deal falls through. Keep it quiet until it's announced.' What's wrong?

Answer: Every classic fraud signal is there: urgency, secrecy, changed bank details, and an unusual channel. The voice being convincing proves nothing in the AI era. The fix is process: call the CEO back on a known number, require a second approver, and verify new bank details with the supplier through contact details already on file.

terms.def: AI-generated fake audio, image or video that imitates a real person.
terms.use: "Treat voice approvals as untrusted; deepfakes make them trivially spoofable."

terms.def: Fraud where attackers impersonate executives or suppliers to trick staff into paying or sharing data.
terms.use: "It's classic BEC, just with an AI-cloned voice instead of an email."

terms.def: Confirming a request through a different, already-trusted channel (e.g. calling a known number).
terms.use: "Any change of bank details needs out-of-band verification before payment."

terms.def: Sign-in methods like passkeys or security keys that can't be tricked into working on a fake site.
terms.use: "Move admins to phishing-resistant MFA; codes by SMS can be phished."

terms.def: Manipulating people, not computers, into breaking security.
terms.use: "AI hasn't changed social engineering's playbook, just made it cheaper to run at scale."

quiz.q: Why is 'look for spelling mistakes' weak advice today?
quiz.why: AI produces natural, error-free text, so judge messages by what they ask you to do instead.

quiz.q: Best defence against a deepfake 'CEO' asking for an urgent transfer?
options: Ask a trick question on the call
Call back on a known number and require a second approver
quiz.why: Process beats perception: independent verification and multi-person approval don't depend on spotting a fake.

quiz.q: How should a security analyst treat an AI tool's alert summary?
options: As a helpful lead to verify
quiz.why: AI can be confidently wrong; use it to go faster, then verify with evidence.

quiz.q: Which MFA is most resistant to AI-powered phishing pages?
quiz.why: Passkeys are bound to the real website, so a fake login page can't use them.

talk.scenario: A colleague says: 'AI hacking is just hype, nothing has really changed.' How do you respond?
talk.model: Partly true: the core attacks such as phishing, BEC and credential theft are the same. What changed is scale and quality. AI removes the tell-tale typos and makes deepfake voice and video cheap, as the Arup case showed with a fake video call. So our controls should shift from 'spot the fake' to verification: out-of-band confirmation, two-person payment approval and phishing-resistant MFA.

reflect: Think of one situation in your own life where you trust a voice or face without checking. How could AI exploit it, and what simple verification habit would protect you?
